The deepsea jewfish Glaucosoma buergeri is a large, slow-growing teleost inhabiting the continental shelf waters of the Indo-West Pacific. Field surveys and otolith-based studies have documented that individuals attain an ultimate standard length of 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the larger members of the Glaucosomatidae. At birth, the wet weight of newly emerged yolk-sac larvae is approximately 0.001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that reflects the tiny pelagic egg diameter of roughly 1.25 millimeters from which they hatch. This minimal larval mass imposes a narrow window for first exogenous feeding, as the lecithotrophic phase is brief and dependent on water temperature. In captivity at a stable 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of this species has been inferred from fecundity estimates of congeneric Glaucosoma scapulare, suggesting that a single gravid female can produce around 1,000,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = around 1,000,000 eggs per spawning event]. Such high fecundity is typical of broadcast spawners that release pelagic eggs into an unpredictable planktonic environment.

Sexual maturation in Glaucosoma buergeri occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to its ultimate dimensions. Based on morphological and gonadal data from Glaucosoma scapulare, the standard length at puberty is estimated at 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 537 grams [Wwp = approximately 537 grams]. This pubertal weight, derived from a length-weight relationship of 0.02399 times length raised to the 2.89 power, represents only about one-fifth of the ultimate wet weight that adults can eventually achieve. The onset of reproductive activity is thus delayed until fish have accumulated substantial somatic reserves, a life-history strategy that is common among demersal reef fishes where body size confers advantages in territory defense and gamete production. Females at this size are reproductively viable, though their contribution to annual recruitment is likely lower than that of the largest individuals in the population, which enjoy disproportionately higher fecundity.

The ultimate wet weight of this species, calculated from the same length-weight relationship applied to the maximum recorded length, reaches 2,570 grams [Wwi = 2,570 grams] in the largest individuals. This substantial adult mass is associated with a relatively protracted lifespan; tag-recapture and otolith annulus analyses indicate that the maximum documented lifespan in the wild is 27 years [am = 27 years], recorded under mean annual water temperatures of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. Such longevity is notable among subtropical serraniform fishes and reflects a slow pace of life, characterized by delayed maturation, moderate somatic growth rates, and iteroparous reproduction over many seasons. The deepsea jewfish appears to channel resources preferentially into structural growth rather than early reproduction, a pattern that buffers population dynamics against recruitment variability but renders the species vulnerable to overfishing of larger, older individuals.

Reproductive output in Glaucosoma buergeri is tied to thermal conditions that govern vitellogenesis and spawning frequency. At the typical summer water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], females have been recorded producing up to 1,000,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = up to 1,000,000 eggs per spawning event], with individual fish capable of multiple spawning events across a single breeding season. Specifically, the spawning frequency under these thermal conditions is approximately once per year [F_R_i = spawning frequency under these thermal conditions is approximately once per year], yielding a daily reproductive rate that sustains high larval output during the peak spawning period. This iteroparous strategy, combined with high fecundity per event, compensates for the substantial mortality experienced during the pelagic larval phase, which may last several weeks before settlement occurs on the outer continental shelf. The energetic demands of such repeated spawning likely constrain growth rates in reproductively active adults.

Comparisons with other members of the Glaucosomatidae highlight the deepsea jewfish's relatively conservative life-history profile. The asymptotic mass of 2,570 grams [Wwi = 2,570 grams] is intermediate among its congeners, with Glaucosoma hebraicum reaching slightly smaller maximum sizes while Glaucosoma scapulare attains comparable dimensions. The lifespan of 27 years [am = 27 years] observed under field conditions at 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C] aligns with the extended longevity documented in other subtropical demersal fishes, which typically exhibit slower metabolic rates than their tropical counterparts. The wet weight at birth of 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams] is similarly typical for pelagic-spawning teleosts with small, transparent eggs. Taken together, the combination of moderate asymptotic size, delayed puberty at 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters] standard length, high fecundity, and exceptional longevity suggests that Glaucosoma buergeri follows a bet-hedging life history in which reproductive effort is spread across many years to buffer against environmental stochasticity in larval survival.
